tldr: Using policies trained purely with deep reinforcement learning in simulation, acrobatic and highly dynamic maneuvers—swinging up onto two front wheels, upright balancing, spinning in place, driving over rough terrain, and landing softly—were fully automated on an operational 5-tonne physical skid-steer loader for the first time.
hero_caption: A suite of acrobatic maneuvers autonomously executed by a physical 5-tonne skid-steer loader using reinforcement learning policies: swinging up onto two front wheels by building momentum (A), driving over 75 cm rough terrain while balancing on two wheels (B), maintaining balance under arm acceleration/deceleration disturbances (C), spinning in place (D), and executing a soft landing that dissipates impact with the ground (E).
overview:
Heavy machinery such as hydraulic excavators and skid-steer loaders (construction vehicles that turn via differential wheel speeds) is attracting significant attention for construction and agricultural automation. However, their complex hydraulic actuation involves strong nonlinearities and delays, making precise first-principles dynamic modeling extremely difficult. Consequently, conventional techniques like Model Predictive Control (MPC) have struggled with extreme dynamic maneuvers where contact conditions change abruptly. Furthermore, because these machines weigh several tonnes, trial-and-error reinforcement learning (RL) on the physical system is impossible due to severe risks of damage.

To address this, the authors proposed an approach combining simulation-based RL with zero-shot transfer to reality (Sim-to-Real). First, from input-output data gathered while driving the physical machine forward and backward, they trained a compact neural network actuator model that captures hydraulic delays and history. They integrated this into a physics simulator alongside a rigid-body model measured simply using a tape measure and platform scales. Next, they decomposed the overall behavior into four sub-skills with overlapping state distributions—swing-up, stabilize, track velocities, and soft landing—and trained each separately via Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) using domain randomization and curriculum learning.

In experiments on a physical 5-tonne John Deere 332G, the system achieved autonomous swing-up onto two front wheels without prior demonstrations, trajectory tracking while upright on two wheels, spinning in place at maximum speed, traversing 75 cm rough terrain, and landing softly without crashing into the ground. While an MPC baseline tipped over during high-speed driving or on rough ground, the RL policies maintained stability, demonstrating the strong generalization and practicality of RL for extreme dynamic control of heavy machinery.
contributions: Demonstrated, for the first time in the world, the fully autonomous execution of a suite of acrobatic maneuvers on an operational 5-tonne hydraulic skid-steer loader, ranging from swinging up onto two front wheels to balanced driving, spinning in place, and soft four-wheel landing.

Established a practical Sim-to-Real pipeline that identifies a neural network actuator model capturing hydraulic delays using platform scales, a tape measure, and short real-world data runs, without relying on prior detailed CAD models or specialized domain expertise.

Introduced a modular control architecture that divides extreme dynamic maneuvers involving abrupt contact changes and nonlinearities into four sub-skills, smoothly connecting them via simple transition rules that leverage overlapping state distributions.
Demonstrated the generality of the method across platforms and drive types (hydraulic vs. electric) by successfully applying the identical pipeline to a compact electric 4WD vehicle (SMB).

sections.heading: Why teach heavy machinery "acrobatics"?
sections.summary: Automating hydraulic heavy equipment is essential for addressing labor shortages and improving safety, but fluid compressibility, hose elasticity, large response delays, and changing contacts make accurate modeling extraordinarily difficult. This study leverages simulation RL and sim-to-real transfer to tackle the full automation of two-wheel acrobatic maneuvers on a 5-tonne machine—feats previously achieved only by elite human operators in world-record performances.
sections.details:
In heavy equipment sectors such as construction and mining, autonomous operation is strongly desired not only to boost productivity, but also to alleviate severe labor shortages and keep workers safe. However, hydraulic drive systems suffer from hydraulic fluid compressibility, flexible hoses, hysteresis, and large response delays, making accurate analytical physics models extremely difficult to construct.

While Model Predictive Control (MPC) has succeeded in settled behaviors such as trajectory tracking, dynamic maneuvers involving discontinuous contact changes and underactuated balancing push non-convex optimization and real-time computation to their limits. Conversely, as demonstrated in recent quadrupedal robots and drones, deep reinforcement learning (RL) combined with sim-to-real transfer has shown remarkable results in complex control involving numerous simultaneous inputs/outputs and frequent contact transitions.

Here, the authors set out to train RL policies on an operational 5-tonne skid-steer loader (John Deere 332G) to perform extreme maneuvers: swinging up onto two front wheels, balancing upright on two wheels, spinning in place, driving over rough undulating terrain, and landing safely back on four wheels. These maneuvers demand the limits of actuation (full torque and maximum velocity) and have historically been accomplished only by a handful of top human operators setting official world records. While appearing to be mere stunts, mastering these skills brings immense practical value—such as enabling loaders to climb autonomously onto trucks without loading ramps, reducing tire scrubbing and ground damage in muddy terrain, negotiating obstacles on rough ground, and self-recovering from being stuck.

sections.heading: A 5-tonne machine airborne: outstanding agility in physical experiments
sections.summary: The learned policies ran on a standard laptop connected to a commercial 5-tonne John Deere 332G fitted with minimal sensors and protective bars. In real-world tests, the RL policies demonstrated agility and robustness that far surpassed an MPC baseline: two-wheel swing-up, impact-mitigating soft landing, velocity tracking, balancing under arm disturbances, spinning in place, and traversing 75 cm rough obstacles.
sections.details:
The experimental platform, a John Deere 332G, is a two-axle, four-wheel hydraulically driven skid-steer loader where cabin joystick commands are converted into left and right wheel speed targets by an onboard low-level controller. In these experiments, the joystick signals were intercepted, wheel encoder values were read from the CAN bus, and control commands were sent from a standard laptop (Intel Core i7, no GPU) using retrofitted IMUs on the base and arm. To prevent structural damage in case of tipping over, a rear wheelie bar and auxiliary bucket wheels were installed, but neither contacts the ground during standard operations.

### Swing-Up and Stabilize
Starting from a standstill on all four wheels, the machine rocks forward and backward to accumulate momentum before swinging up into an upright two-wheel pose. The controller divides this into "swing-up" and "stabilize" phases, switching when the machine pitch angle reaches $-30^\circ$. On the physical machine, a bang-bang pattern (full reverse $\to$ forward $\to$ full reverse) automatically emerged just as in simulation, successfully transitioning to an upright balance. The success rate was extremely high, except under an extreme configuration where the arm was raised far above the training range (the bucket touched the ground in 3 out of 14 trials).

### Soft Landing
This controller safely returns the machine from an upright two-wheel balance back onto all four wheels. If let drop passively (zero command), the 5-tonne vehicle's impact causes the front wheels to bounce violently and destabilizes the body. In contrast, the learned policy commands 100% forward drive to bring the rear wheels down quickly, then instantly switches to 100% reverse right before touchdown to absorb the impact, landing with virtually zero rebound.

### Balance and Track Velocities
For the stationary upright balance task, the RL policy stayed upright with small pitch fluctuations of $\pm 1.6^\circ$, matching the stability of MPC. In a tracking test with step-like target wheel speed increases up to $4\,\mathrm{rad/s}$, MPC lost balance and fell over past $3.5\,\mathrm{rad/s}$, whereas RL tracked target speeds seamlessly up to the actuator limit.

Furthermore, when the loader arm was moved vigorously up and down to drastically shift the center of mass, the RL policy adapted instantly and preserved balance. When commanded to spin in place with a left-right wheel speed difference of up to $8.4\,\mathrm{rad/s}$, it rotated smoothly without tipping. Most impressively, a policy trained exclusively on flat ground was deployed onto rough undulating terrain with 75 cm elevation changes. While MPC became stuck and failed to climb, the RL policy autonomously perceived and compensated for uphill deceleration and downhill gravitational acceleration, driving over the obstacles with ease in both forward and reverse directions.

captions.F3: Execution logs on the real system compared against simulation. In swing-up (A, B), control switches smoothly to the stabilization controller at pitch angle $-30^\circ$. In soft landing (C, D), the impact is dissipated by switching from forward to reverse drive. In-place balancing (E) and velocity tracking (F) also show close agreement between simulation and reality.
captions.F4: Robustness validation on the physical machine. The RL policy maintains balance without tipping across large center-of-mass shifts from dynamic arm movements (A), two-wheel in-place spins with superimposed yaw commands (B), and rough terrain traversal with 75 cm elevations using a policy trained purely on flat ground (C).

sections.heading: Why did RL outperform MPC?
sections.summary: While matching or exceeding MPC on simple tracking tasks, the RL policies clearly surpassed MPC in long-horizon planning, swing-up with contact transitions, and zero-shot generalization from flat ground to rough terrain. Offloading computation to offline simulation training yields a lightweight network ideal for real-time control in unseen conditions.
sections.details:
A notable achievement of this work is deploying policies successfully to a physical heavy machine without prior CAD models or specialized parameter hand-tuning, relying instead on a pragmatic identification procedure and domain randomization. Modularizing the behaviors into distinct sub-skills rather than training a monolithic policy minimized hyperparameter tuning overhead.

Comparing against MPC, both controllers exhibited comparable performance during simple stationary balancing. However, RL proved overwhelmingly superior in maximum trackable velocity and out-of-distribution rough terrain traversal. Because the MPC model did not incorporate environmental geometry, it could not reject the bumps and came to a stop. RL, endowed with robustness through domain randomization, instinctively modulated wheel velocities in response to sensor pitch and velocity deviations, clearing obstacles effortlessly.

Moreover, highly non-convex tasks involving repeated make-and-break contacts, such as swing-up, are difficult for MPC without an explicit contact-sequence planner. RL, on the other hand, acquired dynamic whole-body coordination through the same learning algorithm (PPO) simply by adjusting the reward function and initial state distributions. Additionally, runtime computation on the physical machine requires only a forward pass through a small MLP (under a few milliseconds), bypassing optimization convergence concerns and offering a decisive advantage for field robotics.

Currently, transitions between skills rely on a rule-based state machine, but because the initial state distributions of successive skills are intentionally designed to overlap, transitions remain remarkably robust. Looking ahead, pairing these controllers with a higher-level decision-making policy (hierarchical RL) could enable longer, more complex autonomous missions, such as ramp-less truck loading.

sections.heading: The core of Sim-to-Real: hydraulic actuator learning and reward design
sections.summary: The cornerstone of the methodology is combining a neural network actuator model learned from physical operational data with a rigid-body model approximated via platform scale measurements. Using PPO, four subtasks—swing-up, stabilize, velocity tracking, and landing—were trained in simulation using tailored reward functions and curriculum learning.
sections.details:
The complete workflow consists of four steps: rigid-body modeling, actuator identification, simulation RL, and physical deployment.

### Actuator Model & Rigid-Body Model
The primary hurdle with hydraulic actuators lies in their latency and nonlinear dynamics. The authors observed that commanding identical inputs produced virtually the same response speeds whether the wheels spun freely in the air or drove the full 5-tonne vehicle on the ground. In other words, the system behaves as a velocity-controlled system where wheel velocity is uniquely determined by the command history. They collected 1.5 hours of driving data using random step and sinusoidal inputs, then trained a 3-layer fully connected neural network (with SoftSign activations) that takes past control inputs and wheel speeds (over 1.8 seconds, 30 points) to predict the wheel velocity 20 ms ahead. For the rigid-body model, without using CAD, they built a simplified model of boxes and cylinders using dimensions measured by tape and center-of-mass/mass figures derived from moment balance on a commercial truck scale.

### Reinforcement Learning & Subtasks
Simulations were run in RaiSim, and policies were trained with PPO. The observation space included pitch angle, pitch rate, average wheel speed, and past action history, injected with Gaussian noise matching physical sensor tolerances. Mass and inertia were sampled uniformly each episode for domain randomization.

- ### Swing-Up: To generate rocking momentum, the policy was rewarded for large positive and negative pitch angles, while excessive backward pitch (rear body contact) was penalized increasingly via curriculum learning. This allowed the policy to first leverage ground contact before learning to lift up purely on momentum without scraping.
- ### Stabilize and Balance: Episodes started near a $-30^\circ$ pitch angle following swing-up, terminating early on tipping or bucket ground contact, encouraging smooth, low-effort balancing actions.
- ### Soft Landing: When lowering the rear wheels from an upright stance, the policy received rewards as pitch approached $0^\circ$ and penalties if the front wheels rebounded upward, automatically inducing a counter-thrust (full reverse) right before touchdown.
- ### Balance and Track Velocities: A squared error penalty against target wheel speeds was introduced via curriculum learning: the policy focused first on balance before tracking weights were phased in. On the physical system, a first-order low-pass filter (coefficient $\beta=0.8$) was applied to the policy output to ensure smooth behavior.

captions.F5: Overall pipeline of the proposed methodology. A neural network actuator model predicts future velocity from past inputs and wheel speeds measured on the real machine (A) and is embedded in simulation. Leveraging the observation that wheel responses are nearly identical under no-load vs. loaded conditions (B), the resulting model closely mirrors physical machine behavior (C).
captions.F6: Reinforcement learning training design and learning curves. Initial state distributions for each sub-skill (A), vehicle pitch postures (B), and reward shapes (C) are defined. For swing-up (D) and velocity tracking (H), curriculum learning effectively aids initial exploration before tightening constraints.

sections.heading: Supplementary details: MPC baseline and transfer to a small electric vehicle
sections.summary: The baseline MPC was formulated as a planar inverted pendulum on a cart with a first-order lag actuator. To verify generality, the same framework was applied to a 100 kg electric 4WD vehicle, the "Super Mega Bot," achieving robust two-wheel balancing capable of rejecting human kicks and rough terrain.
sections.details:
### SSL Model Predictive Control Baseline
The comparative MPC baseline modeled the machine as a planar inverted pendulum (four states: wheel position $x$, wheel speed $v$, pitch angle $\theta$, and pitch rate $\dot{\theta}$) with the front wheels treated as a cylinder and the vehicle as a lumped mass. Actuators were modeled as a first-order delay with time constant $T$ obtained via system identification. CasADi solved the nonlinear optimization over a 40-step horizon (0.8 seconds ahead at 0.02 s intervals). Because MPC cannot handle contact discontinuities, it cannot perform swing-up or soft landing; it was initialized only after human operators manually pitched the machine into an upright stance.

### Case Study: Super Mega Bot (SMB)
To show that the approach does not depend on hydraulic drive or a 5-tonne form factor, the framework was extended to a 100 kg electric 4WD vehicle, the Super Mega Bot (SMB). Unlike the velocity-controlled hydraulic loader, the SMB uses torque control. An actuator model was trained to predict torque from command history using torque estimated from mass and flat-ground accelerations. Due to its light weight and low inertia, the SMB requires significantly faster and finer control responses.

In physical tests, the policy trained purely in simulation restored balance even when kicked forcefully and pushed several meters by a human, and successfully drove over gravel and steps with intuitive velocity tracking where steering and forward drive were decoupled. This confirms that the framework serves as a versatile solution for extreme dynamic balancing across diverse mobility platforms and actuation types, from heavy equipment to compact exploration robots.

captions.F7: Planar inverted pendulum model of the skid-steer loader used in the MPC baseline. The front wheels are modeled as a cylinder and the entire machine body, including the arm, is treated as a single rigid body with pitch inertia to derive the equations of motion.

takeaways: Severe hydraulic actuation delays and nonlinearities can be bridged for extreme Sim-to-Real maneuvers simply by training a small MLP on history data collected during short physical runs.

Even without CAD models or high-precision parameter identification, combining rudimentary tools (tape measures and platform scales) with domain randomization is fully sufficient for real-world deployment.

For ultra-dynamic tasks involving abrupt contact changes, dividing the problem into overlapping sub-skills with simple transition logic is far more robust and efficient than solving everything with a single policy.
The framework applies out of the box not only to 5-tonne hydraulic heavy machinery but also to 100 kg electric 4WD robots, demonstrating a platform-agnostic solution for extreme dynamic control.
limitations: The machine lacks exteroceptive sensors like cameras or LiDAR; rough terrain traversal relies purely on the policy's blind proprioceptive robustness, preventing proactive trajectory optimization over known terrain profiles.

Under extreme conditions where the arm is raised higher than the training distribution, increased inertia can prevent the machine from decelerating in time during swing-up, resulting in occasional bucket ground contact.

Transitions between sub-skills are currently governed by rule-based state machines keyed to pitch and velocity thresholds; higher-level hierarchical RL will be needed to orchestrate complex, long-duration autonomous workflows.
